name: Nightmare
description: The mare — a female demon of Germanic and Slavic folklore that rides sleepers' chests, causing sleep paralysis and bad dreams. The original referent of the modern English word 'nightmare'.
full_description: The original 'nightmare' was not a bad dream but a being: the mare (Old English mære, Old Norse mara, Proto-Germanic *marōn), a female nocturnal demon believed to sit, walk, or 'ride' on the chest of a sleeper, producing the sensation of suffocation and inability to move that we now identify as sleep paralysis. The English word 'nightmare' generalised from this experience to any bad dream around 1829. The mare appears across Germanic and Slavic Europe with consistent phenomenology and rich variation: in Norse tradition she is the mara of the 13th-century Ynglinga saga, who 'rides' King Vanlandi to death; in German folklore she is closely related to the alp (German Albtraum, 'alp-dream'); in Polish and Czech tradition the zmora/můra causes nightmares and is associated with moths. Protective practices were common, including charms, plugged carpenter-holes, and overturned brooms. The word's Indo-European root *mer- evokes 'crushing, pressing, oppressing', mirroring the bodily experience itself.

aliases.name: Mare
aliases.language: Old English / Old Norse / Common Germanic

origin: Germanic and Slavic Europe; the mare and her cognates are documented across Scandinavia, the Low Countries, German-speaking Europe, the British Isles, and Slavic lands.

etymology.origin: From Old English mære, mare, cognate with Old Norse mara, German Mahr, Dutch (nacht)merrie; ultimately from Proto-Germanic *marōn and Proto-Indo-European *mer- ('crush, press, oppress'). No etymological connection to the modern English 'mare' (female horse).
etymology.meaning: Originally the female demon of sleep oppression; later, the bad dream associated with her
etymology.first_use: Old English mære attested in early medieval texts; English 'nightmare' generalised to any bad dream by c. 1829

timeline.event: Snorri Sturluson, in the Ynglinga saga, records the death of King Vanlandi of Uppsala at the hands of a mara summoned by the Finnish sorceress Huld at the request of his abandoned wife Drífa
timeline.significance: Earliest detailed literary account of the mara; foundational reference for Norse mare-tradition

timeline.event: Henry Fuseli paints The Nightmare, depicting an incubus-like figure crouched on a sleeping woman
timeline.significance: Iconic visual codification of the mare/incubus motif in Western art

timeline.event: English 'nightmare' generalises from sleep paralysis specifically to any bad dream
timeline.source: Standard English etymological dictionaries (cited via Wikipedia)

timeline.event: Jacob Grimm publishes Deutsche Mythologie, providing extensive documentation of the mare across Germanic tradition

related.name: Night Hag
related.description: Cross-cultural sleep-paralysis figure; the night-hag and the mare share phenomenology

related.name: Alp
related.description: German nightmare-causing entity; closely entwined with the mare in folk tradition

cultural_notes: Across Germanic and Slavic Europe the mare was treated as a real being; protective practices included charms, plugged carpenter-holes, brooms placed upside-down at doors, knives, and overturned slippers.
